blocks.text: Pacinian receptors are rapidly adapting receptors sensitive to vibrations and rapid pressure changes

**Adaptation of receptors:** One of the most important characteristics of sensory receptors is that they can adapt partially or completely to any constant stimulus after a period of time. When a continuous stimulus is applied to a receptor, the initial response occurs at a high impulse rate, then at a progressively slower rate, which ultimately decreases to very few or none at all.
**Mechanism:** Adaptation occurs in 2 ways:

items.text: **1 In Rapidly Adapting Receptors** It is a faster mechanism. The receptors are viscoelastic in nature so that when a stimulus is applied to one side of the receptor, it is transmitted instantly by the viscous component to the same side of the central nerve fiber, eliciting a response Within a few seconds, the fluid in the receptors redistributes and the response is no longer elicited

**2 In Slowly Adapting Receptors** It is a slower mechanism called accommodation This occurs directly in the nerve fiber. If there is a continued stimulus, then the tip of the receptor becomes accommodated to the stimulus. This occurs from the progressive inactivation of sodium channels in the nerve fiber membrane.
**Rapidly adapting receptors** Pacinian, Meissner’s and hearing organ
**Slow adapting receptors** Merkel’s, Ruffini’s and free nerve endings (Option A & C ruled out)

blocks.text: Meissner’s corpuscles (Option B) are also rapidly adapting receptors but are sensitive to light touch rather than vibrations.
Receptor potential is the graded depolarizing potential in a sensory receptor in response to a stimulus. Its magnitude varies with the intensity of the stimulus.
Receptor Potentials
A receptor potential is a type of graded potential that occurs in sensory receptors. It is a local, non-propagated change in membrane potential that occurs in response to a stimulus.

Receptor potential is not an action potential; instead, it causes the sensory neuron to fire action potentials. Once the receptor potential reaches a critical threshold, it triggers an action potential at the sensory nerve's first node of Ranvier.
Factors affecting receptor potential:

items.text: **Proportional Response:** Amplitude of receptor potential is generally proportional to stimulus intensity.
**Nature:** Non-propagated, depolarizing potential in sensory receptors.
**Threshold:** When it reaches a critical level, an action potential is generated.
**Stimulus Intensity:** Stronger stimuli lead to larger receptor potentials.

blocks.text: Mechanism of receptor potential generation in Pacinian Corpuscle

rows: Pressure deforms lamellae surrounding sensory nerve ending.
Deformation opens mechanically-gated ion channels, mainly sodium (Na+).
Rapid influx of Na+ generates the receptor potential.
Larger deformation (stronger stimulus) leads to a larger receptor potential.
If the potential reaches ~10 mV, an action potential is generated at the first Node of Ranvier.

items.text: **First-order neurons** Originate in mechanoreceptors, and enter spinal cord via dorsal roots Pseudo-unipolar neurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion Split into medial and lateral branches: Medial branch: Travels up dorsal column to brain Lateral branch: Synapses in dorsal horn, forming local reflexes, spinocerebellar tracts Fibers from lower thoracic, sacral, and lumbar regions (T7-T12, L, S) ascend to medulla without synapsing, forming the fasciculus gracilis Fibers from cervical and upper thoracic regions (C, T1-T6) ascend to medulla without synapsing, forming the fasciculus cuneatus
**Second-order neurons** Synapse in dorsal medulla (cuneate nucleus for upper body, gracile nucleus for lower body) Cross to opposite brain stem side, travel to thalamus (medial lemniscus)
**Third-order neurons** Synapse in thalamus (ventrobasal complex) Project to somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, lateral parietal cortex)
**Nucleus cuneatus:** Transmits sensory information from the upper body (arms and upper torso). The patient's symptoms do not involve these areas. (Option A)
**Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL):** Located in the thalamus, not the medulla. This option is incorrect because the lesion is in the medulla. (Option C)
**Nucleus ambiguus:** Involved in motor control of the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles. It is not related to the dorsal column pathway or the sensory symptoms described. (Option D)

Anterolateral Pathway

Transmits sensory signals such as pain, temperature, crude touch, itch, sexual sensations, and crude pressure from the opposite side of the body. Damage results in loss of pain and temperature sensation on the opposite side below the lesion.
**Characteristics:** Slower transmission, less precise spatial localization, reduced ability to transmit rapidly changing signals.
**Pathway: Origin and Path** Sensory signals enter the spinal cord via dorsal roots; and originate from nociceptors, thermoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.

items.text: **First Order Neurons** Afferent fibers with cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (DRG); terminate in the dorsal horn.

**Second Order Neurons** Cell bodies in laminae I, II, and V of the dorsal horn; axons cross the midline and ascend in the anterolateral funiculus. Synapses with VPL of the thalamus Crude Touch Fibers -Form the anterior spinothalamic tract. Pain and Temperature Fibers - Form the lateral spinothalamic tract.
**Third Order Neurons** Originate from VPL, midline, and intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus; project to specific sensory cortex areas.

blocks.text: **Termination Points** Reticular nuclei of the brainstem; Thalamus: Ventrobasal complex (tactile signals) and intralaminar nuclei (pain signals).

Cortical plasticity

Refers to the ability of neurons to modify their connections under specific circumstances. Cortical structures are capable of reorganization (plasticity) after loss of a body part, neighboring areas take over the cortical area of the lost part. (Option A). Cortical connections of sensory units become weak with disuse and strengthen with use.
Phantom Limb Pain

Perceived due to cortical plasticity In the phantom limb phenomenon, the limb actually does not exist (amputated), but the patient complains that he feels pain or itch in the limb Based on the evidence, brain reorganization occurs when sensory input is cut off.
**For example:** In leg amputees, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus can perceive the signal that once received input from leg and foot now responds to stump (thigh) stimulation
**Management:**

items.text: **Epidural Anesthesia:** Used during amputation surgery to reduce acute pain and subsequent need for opioids, lowering phantom pain incidence.
**Spinal Cord Stimulation:** Electric current stimulates spinal pathways, reducing phantom limb pain and causing a tingling sensation instead in phantom limb (Option A)

blocks.text: The law of Projection forms the basis of phantom limb
Laws of Sensory Physiology

items.text: **Bell-Magendie Law:** States that the dorsal root of the spinal cord is sensory and the ventral root of the spinal cord is motor in function. (Option B)

**Muller's Doctrine of Specific Nerve Energy:** States that sensation evoked by a stimulus that generates impulse in the specific sensory pathway depends on the precise area of the brain that is eventually activated by the stimulus. (Option A)

**Law of Projection:** States that no matter where a specific sensory pathway is stimulated along its course to the cortex, the sensation is referred to the location of the receptors. Forms the basis of the phantom limb. (Option C)

**Weber-Fechner Law:** States that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the logarithm of the intensity of the stimulus. (Option D) Interpreted signal strength = Log (Stimulus) + Constant Emphasizes that the greater the background sensory intensity, the greater an additional change must be for the individual to detect the change.

blocks.text: **Labelled Line Theory** States that each sensory receptor is specialized to detect specific stimuli and sends signals via dedicated nerve fibers to the corresponding area of the somatosensory cortex.

blocks.text: Corticospinal tract: The corticospinal tract, also known as the pyramidal tract, is the most important descending tract from the motor cortex.

blocks.text: After leaving the cortex, the tract passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, then through the brainstem and into the medulla.

In the medulla, most of the fibers cross to the opposite side, forming the medullary pyramids. These crossed fibers descend as the lateral corticospinal tract finally terminates in the spinal cord. Some fibers which do not cross to the opposite side in the medulla pass ipsilaterally down to the spinal cord as the ventral corticospinal tract.
